title: Wedding invitation words that feel like you
excerpt: A warm opening, the right family details, and one clear place for every function. Start with what your guests need, then add your voice.

sections.heading: Begin with a welcome, not a rulebook
paragraphs: Your invitation can sound like a conversation with someone you love. Start with a short line that feels natural when you say it aloud. ‘Together with our families’ suits a shared family invitation; ‘We’re getting married!’ feels more personal and direct. Neither needs to become a long formal announcement.

If you prefer Hinglish, keep it easy to read. A familiar phrase can carry more warmth than several decorative quotations. Choose the language because it feels right to you, rather than because of the design you selected.
sections.quote: Shaadi apni, khushiyaan sabki. Hamari new beginning mein aapka hona banta hai!

sections.heading: Give each function its own details
paragraphs: A guest should be able to tell which day and venue belong to each function without reading your whole story. List the ceremony, meal and other gatherings separately when their times or locations differ. Use the names your families actually use for those occasions.

Write an arrival time when it differs from the ceremony time. Add the city and a useful landmark alongside the map link, especially when the venue has several entrances. A short dress note can help, but include one only if you want guests to follow it.
list: Check every date, time and timezone.
Spell names and venue details as the hosts want them shown.
Keep private or restricted functions out of the general schedule.
Make directions and the RSVP route easy to find.

sections.heading: Leave room for your own family
paragraphs: Family names, blessings and ceremonial wording are optional. Include the people and phrases you want, and remove anything that does not represent your celebration. A wedding invitation does not need to assume a religion or a particular family structure.

Before sharing, ask one person to read it on a phone. Let them find the date, venue and response option without hints. Then read the welcome aloud once more: the final invitation should feel as clear as it feels personal.
